articles.title: Poll: Most voters say Trump has hurt the economy as competitive midterm election looms
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s sinking ratings threaten to drag down Republicans in November’s midterm elections, as voters blame him for high prices and a shaky economy, according to a new NBC News poll. The president’s approval rating stands at 41% among registered voters, a second-term low in the poll, with a majority (55%) of voters saying they believe Trump’s policies have hurt the economy. That’s up from 48% in March, before the Iran war pushed up prices on gas and other goods and cemented the rising cost of living as voters’ most pressing issue. Democrats hold a 5-point edge in the battle for control of Congress, 50%-45% — not nearly as large a lead as the 12-point advantage the party enjoyed at this point before the 2018 election, when Democrats rode an anti-Trump wave to the House majority in his first midterm as president. Despite that lead, the Democratic Party is still viewed more negatively than Trump and the GOP. That could help Republicans, along with the fact that the fight for control of the House and especially the Senate is playing out in traditionally Republican parts of the country. Democrats would have to flip multiple states Trump carried by double digits in 2024 to win the Senate. “We have a classic battle between these numbers and the political geography in which this campaign will be decided,” said Republican pollster Bill McInturff of Public Opinion Strategies, whose firm conducted the survey alongside Democratic firm Hart Research Associates. “And the Republicans are still standing because of the geography in which this election will be won or lost.” Still, the poll suggests an increasingly gloomy political environment for the GOP. Longtime double-digit leads over the Democratic Party on who would better handle inflation and the economy have evaporated. More than 6 in 10 voters say the Iran war has not been worth it. Voters don’t appear to be motivated by Trump’s signature tax and spending legislation he championed last year. Instead, Trump himself is a powerful motivating factor, but more for Democrats than for Republicans, as more voters — including nearly half of independents — say they consider their vote a signal of opposition to the president than at any other time in three decades of NBC News polling before midterm elections. “Donald Trump has achieved his goal of making this election about him at a historic level. The problem for Trump and Republicans on the ballot in November is that he has also made history in the highest share of voters who say their vote is in opposition to Trump,” said Democratic pollster Jeff Horwitt of Hart Research Associates. Republicans on the campaign trail are trying to shore up their standing by arguing that Democrats are too extreme to trust with congressional majorities. But the poll indicates voters are more anxious about restraining Trump: 50% say they’re more concerned that Republicans will go too far in supporting Trump if they keep control of Congress, while 42% are more concerned Democrats will obstruct the president if they win control of Congress. Independents lean 45%-30% toward greater concern that Republicans will go too far supporting Trump. McInturff acknowledged the challenges for the GOP posed by the political environment, even as the party’s geographic advantages keep Democrats fighting on their turf. “The issue environment is tilting substantially towards the Democrats,” McInturff said. Trump’s struggles continue A majority of voters, 56%, disapprove of Trump’s job performance, including overwhelming shares of Democrats and independents and 16% of Republicans. The share of voters who strongly approve of Trump, 25%, is the second-lowest mark recorded in the NBC News poll across Trump’s first and second terms. The disapproval rating closely tracks the 55% who say Trump’s policies have hurt the economy, while 26% say they have helped and 18% say they have not made much of a difference. At this point in the 2018 election cycle, more voters said Trump’s policies helped the economy (41%) than hurt (26%). And the survey suggests some of Trump’s signature economic policies are falling flat. While Republicans are touting Trump’s signature tax cut and spending measure known as the “big, beautiful bill,” which was enacted in 2025, 42% of voters say they are less likely to support a candidate backing the measure, while 36% say they are more likely to support such a candidate. Trump’s latest gambit — an announcement at the recent Republican convention that he wanted to issue $5,000 payments to every adult if Republicans keep control of Congress — isn’t garnering much interest. While 21% of voters say they’re more likely to back a candidate who supports Trump’s plan, 46% say they’d be less likely. A plurality of Republicans say it would make no difference in their vote choice, while Democrats are uniformly against the idea and 45% of independents would be less likely to support a candidate in favor of the plan. Among independents, 13% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate who backs Trump’s plan. Voters are also continuing to express opposition to the Iran war, with 57% saying they are less likely to support a candidate who supports the war, versus 24% who are more likely to support that candidate. One-third of voters say the war has been worth it, while 62% disagree. And Democrats also have a 4-point advantage, within the poll’s margin of error, on the question of which party voters say they trust to handle the war with Iran. Trump has continued to insert himself into the midterms, including endorsing nearly all Republicans in competitive congressional races. But 52% of voters are less likely to support a candidate endorsed by Trump, while 30% are more likely to support a Trump-backed candidate. Democratic opportunities — and challenges Clear dissatisfaction with the president opens the door for Democrats as they fight for control of Congress this fall. Forty-three percent of registered voters say their vote for Congress is intended to signal opposition to Trump, while 27% say they plan to vote to send a signal of support for Trump and 28% say their vote won’t be a signal either way. Among independents, almost half (46%) see their vote as a signal of opposition to Trump, while just a handful (10%) say their vote is a signal of support for the president. Democrats have a 1-point lead when voters are asked which party they trust more in dealing with the economy — a result within the poll’s margin of error. It’s the third consecutive NBC News poll with both parties sitting about even on that question. In the same survey just three years ago, Republicans enjoyed a 21-point advantage when it came to handling the economy. Democrats also have a 7-point edge on controlling inflation, as well as slight leads on dealing with the war in Iran and dealing with corruption — government corruption was the second-most popular choice when voters were asked to rank the most important issue facing the country, with concern about the issue heightened among members of both parties and independents. The Democratic Party also has double-digit leads on dealing with data centers and dealing with healthcare. Republicans still hold significant advantages over Democrats on handling crime, border security and immigration, including a 21-point lead on border security. But that is down from the 36-point edge the GOP held over Democrats on the issue in Sept. 2022, after Trump has made aggressive immigration enforcement a hallmark of his second term. Democrats also have a narrow lead on interest in the election, as well as among party identification. But it’s not all rosy for the opposition party. The Republican Party is viewed more positively by voters: 36% have a positive view of the GOP, while 49% view the party negatively. On the Democratic Party, voters are split 29%-50%. Meanwhile, the Democratic Socialists of America is viewed positively by 22% of voters, as Republicans try to link other Democrats to the left-wing group, which rose in prominence following some major primary wins in the past two years. One poll respondent — Aidan Valenzuela, a 19-year-old Texan who doesn’t affiliate with either party — told NBC News that he hasn’t plugged into the election yet and is still unsure whom he’ll vote for. But he said his father grew up during the Cold War and that he’s wary of Democrats who describe themselves as democratic socialists. “Any relation toward socialism or communism in general gives me the ick. It’s like a buzzword that generally just makes me not want to sway in that direction,” he said. Half of voters say they’d be less likely to vote for a candidate who “supports many of the Democratic Socialists of America’s proposed policies,” while 31% say they’d be more likely to support those kinds of candidates. Candidates calling to abolish ICE, a big point of emphasis among progressives, draw similarly unpopular scores with voters. That said, for all the Democratic infighting over policies like “Medicare for All,” 53% of voters say they would be more likely to support a candidate who favors the policy, while 36% said it would make them less likely to vote for that candidate. When asked a similar question with slightly different wording to note the healthcare would be financed in part by taxes, 49% say they’d be more likely to support a candidate that backed the policy and 39% say they’d be less likely. Horwitt, the Democratic pollster, noted that his party “remains in a terrible position as a brand nationally,” even as the poll paints a dismal picture for Trump and Republicans. “This speaks more to deep dissatisfaction with Trump and Republicans than a ringing endorsement of Democrats,” he said. “The party in power does not have a positive story to tell on the major issues of the day: inflation, corruption and the Iran war. Voters are continuing to look for change.” The NBC News poll surveyed 1,000 registered voters Sept. 11-15 via a mix of telephone interviews and an online survey sent via text message. The margin of error is plus or minus 3.1 percentage points.

articles.title: Trump is only amping up his antics ahead of the midterm election
articles.summary: While President Donald Trump’s personal behavior is often strange, his conduct over the last 10 days have been pretty remarkable — especially with the midter...
articles.body:
While President Donald Trump's personal behavior is often strange, his conduct over the last 12 days has been pretty remarkable — especially with the midterm election around the corner.

He's offered voters what even some Republicans say amounts to a bribe. He's threatened (jokingly?) to withhold disaster aid from a state if it doesn't elect a GOP senator. Ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, he told a dubious story about his proximity to Ground Zero . He's baselessly suggested Democrats conspired to kill him. He's threatened to halt all foreign trade. He's holding the future of the Kennedy Center hostage if judges don't allow him to put his name on it, and says he wants his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch across Arlington National Cemetery to double as a military complex housing drones and snipers. He's also now denying certain media outlets , including CNN, access to the White House.

One of the most underestimated reasons for the decline in Trump's political fortunes is Americans' loss of faith in his leadership capabilities.

67% of Americans said he doesn't carefully consider important decisions.

And more than 7 in 10 adults and registered voters said he doesn't even have a plan for the Iran war, according to both Fox News and CNN polling.

And in the runup to the 2026 midterm elections, he's doing very little to disabuse people of these notions.

Trump's offer of $5,000 to every adult US citizen if Republicans keep their House and Senate majorities is certainly a quid pro quo. Registered voters say 66%-18% that it's "inappropriate."

His joke-y threat Wednesday to withhold disaster aid from North Carolina if it elects a Democratic senator is also eyebrow-raising. Trump said he was kidding, but his track record makes clear his administration has discriminated against blue states on such things. And it's a pretty unfunny thing to even joke about.

His tale ahead of the 9/11 anniversary about firefighters carrying him away amid fears of a building collapse was unconfirmed and misleading at best, as CNN's Daniel Dale wrote . And to the extent the story is embellished, it sounds a lot like the president stealing valor.

Trump also claimed this week that the 2024 assassination attempt against him in Butler, Pennsylvania, was " a Democrat Plot, to get me out of the Election " — an explosive claim, if there were any truth to it. But there remains no evidence that any Democrats were involved and he didn't provide any more detail. Indeed, attempted assassin Thomas Crooks was a registered Republican. And even the same day as Trump's comments, FBI Director Kash Patel testified that there was "no evidence" that Crooks "was literally even speaking to any other human being other than his parents."

Trump repeatedly threatened to halt large portions of US foreign trade — including with all countries with whom the US has a trade deficit — if the Federal Reserve doesn't lower interest rates. "If we stop trading with every country that we have a deficit with, which is most of them, and which would be very easy to do, we'd make at least $1.5 trillion a year," Trump claimed Wednesday in North Carolina. That logic makes no sense .

By Friday, Trump suddenly announced he was "banning" CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House "effective immediately," catching even some of his own staff off guard. A CNN reporter was denied access to White House grounds Saturday morning and her press pass was seized. A reporter for Politico and a reporter and photographer for MS NOW were also denied access.

Some of the other examples of Trump's behavior are a little more small-bore, but curious nonetheless.

Trump on Tuesday suggested the Supreme Court justices he nominated might have misrepresented their intentions, saying that they were " not the people I interviewed " and "are merely a shell of their original selves." He broke with longstanding US foreign policy protocol by praising the prospect of the reunification of Ireland. He called concerns about AI safety a "hoax" despite large swaths of Americans being quite concerned about that topic.

And finally, Trump has spent much of this week angling for a way to force the courts to let him put his name on the Kennedy Center, despite that being apparently illegal. Trump is now explicitly suggesting he might let the institution wither and die if he doesn't get what he wants .

It seems like a long time ago, but the talk during Trump's first term was often about his "temperament" and his tweets. His conduct has surely desensitized Americans to some degree.

But these seem like the kinds of behaviors he'd want to rein in ahead of a midterm election where his party's grip on power is on the line and voters have real doubts about his steadiness as a leader.

Trump has gone in the other direction, by upping the antics.

This story has been updated with additional details.

President Donald Trump's approval rating dropped in a new NBC News poll , and more voters criticized his handling of the economy, as the closely watched midterm elections approach.

Trump's approval rating hit a second-term low in the poll at 41% among registered voters, and 55% of voters said they think his policies have hurt the economy. The survey was released on Sept. 20.

In March, 48% of voters told NBC that they believe Trump has hurt the economy, and they ranked the cost of living as their most pressing issue facing the nation in March and September. NBC pollsters noted that the ongoing Iran war has driven up gasoline prices and other costs.

articles.title: Sen. John Barrasso says Trump isn’t violating the Constitution by banning reporters from the White House
articles.summary: Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., on Sunday downplayed concerns that Trump may have violated the Constitution Friday when reporters from Politico, MS NOW and CNN were banned from covering the White House.
articles.body: Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., on Sunday downplayed concerns that President Donald Trump may have violated the Constitution when reporters from Politico, MS NOW and CNN were banned from covering the White House on Saturday. Asked directly whether the president had violated the Constitution, Barrasso said, “No, I believe the press has an obligation to report fairly.” Pressed again on whether he agreed with Trump’s ban, Barrasso said, “We all respect and value the freedom of the press — it’s in the Constitution.” “He was banned from Twitter. He was banned from Facebook, and I didn’t see people come to his defense,” the Wyoming senator told NBC News’ “Meet the Press.” “So it goes both ways. The press has an obligation to report fairly, and the president doesn’t see it happening that way.” Pressed on whether the president’s decision to ban the reporters from White House coverage violated the First Amendment, Barrasso demurred, saying again, “I believe the press has an obligation to report fairly.” He added that he believes Trump’s decision to bar those outlets from the White House would not negatively affect Republicans running for office in the upcoming midterm elections. “The bottom line on all of this is: This is not going to have an impact on an election 44 days from now,” Barrasso said. “People are going to go to the voting booth. They’re going to make a decision based on their life, their future, what they believe is best for them and their families.” The president announced Friday that he was barring three outlets from the White House, writing in a post on Truth Social that he made the decision “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” The president also warned that “other outlets” could face similar action but did not name them. “Media Outlets shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES when they’re covering the President of the United States, the Trump Administration, or the United States of America,” Trump added. Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office on Friday, the president said it wasn’t one particular story that led to his decision, but “cumulative stories over the last few years.” Journalists from the affected outlets reported that they were turned away at the White House security kiosk on Saturday and their credentials were revoked On Saturday, during an MS NOW broadcast, anchor Peter Alexander said that the ban was out of the ordinary. “This is not business as usual. What’s happening right now is different. The latest threat against our cherished freedoms, protected by the U.S. Constitution,” Alexander said. On his show, Alexander interviewed Gabe Rottman, vice president of policy for the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press. Asked whether the ban was legal, Rottman said, “In a word, no.” “The fact that the White House would put the affected news organizations to the task of having to go to court and vindicate their rights, you know that in and of itself is an effort to intimidate the press writ large,” he added. Representatives for Politico, MS NOW and CNN pledged to continue covering the White House despite the bans. “POLITICO will continue to fairly report on this White House and future ones. We will vigorously defend our First Amendment rights against any attempt to restrict them,” the outlet’s press team wrote in a post on X. “We have a right under the U.S. Constitution to do our reporting without hinderance or interference from the government and this ban is an illegal assault on this fundamental right,” CNN said in a statement posted on X. “We will not be deflected from our duty to hold the government and other public bodies to account, and we will continue to report on the actions and processes of this administration without fear or favor,” the statement added. “MS NOW intends to take any and all steps necessary to defend our First Amendment rights and the essential role of independent journalists in our democracy,” the network said in its own statement. The White House Correspondents’ Association, a group that represents the coalition of news outlets and reporters who cover the White House, also denounced the move. “The Constitution protects the freedom of the press from government interference. That protection does not depend on whether the president likes a news organization’s coverage, agrees with its reporting, or approves of the questions its journalists ask,” Jacqui Heinrich, the group’s president, said in a statement. Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., appeared after Barrasso on “Meet the Press” and said banning certain news outlets from the White House violates the First Amendment. “It clearly does,” the New Jersey senator said. “This president has no regard for the First Amendment,” he added. “He’s going after reporters, and this ban just doubles down on that.”

articles.title: Waltz says Trump ‘absolutely within his rights’ to bar reporters ‘not behaving’ in good faith
articles.summary: U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz on Sunday said President Trump is “absolutely within his rights” to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from the White House, claiming the ban prevents reporters who are “not behaving” in good faith. “Dana, the president is absolutely within his rights to limit journalists to government…
articles.body:
U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz on Sunday said President Trump is “absolutely within his rights” to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters from the White House, claiming the ban prevents reporters who are “not behaving” in good faith.

“Dana, the president is absolutely within his rights to limit journalists to government facilities, particularly when, in his opinion, they’re not behaving as good faith journalists,” Waltz told CNN’s Dana Bash on “State of the Union.”

Bash pushed back, stating that as a decorated veteran and former Green Beret, Waltz defended the rights endowed in the Constitution before reiterating Trump’s ban on the three outlets from covering the White House.

“Dana, the prior administration limited all kinds of journalistic outfits and journalists themselves that they deemed as right-wing,” Waltz said. “Those have now been allowed onto the facility, and the president doesn’t believe others are acting in good faith.”

Waltz later added that he hopes the media “would take a good introspective look at itself and its practices,” saying that it makes “a little baby correction” to stories that stick “to people like napalm.” He said there was a difference between what he characterized as “negative reporting and garbage gossip journalism.”

The ambassador pushed back on reporting on U.S. military deployments and the country’s munition stockpile, prompting Bash to say that reporting on national security is something “every serious news organization takes seriously.”

“That is quite different from the president saying that he’s not happy because it’s too negative against him,” she added before moving on to talk about the U.S.’s new deal with Greenland and Denmark.

Trump announced the ban via Truth Social on Friday, posting that it went into immediate effect “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He later said there was no particular reason for the timing of the ban.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday. All three outlets denounced the ban , and MS NOW said it will “take any and all steps necessary” to protect its reporters’ constitutional right to report on the president. Politico editor-in-chief Jonathan Greenberger said the Secret Service confiscated reporter Cheyenne Haslett’s pass.

Several free-speech advocacy groups and press organizations, including Fox News contributors , slammed the ban, calling it a violation of these outlets’ right to press freedom.

The Biden administration previously tightened the requirements for White House passes to reporters, Snopes reported , in March 2025. Citing Politico , the fact-checker stated that the number of passes dropped from 1,417 to 975 after those requirements went into effect due to reporters choosing to not renew their passes. One application for a pass was denied.

Journalists Max Blumenthal and Sam Husseini were escorted out of a State Department press briefing in January 2025, in the last days of the Biden administration. Both confronted former Secretary of State Antony Blinken over the administration’s handling of Israel’s war in Gaza, with Husseini screaming that Blinken belonged “in the Hague.”

articles.title: Trump says his proposed arch will include a military complex housing drones and snipers
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said in a Sunday Truth Social post that he would convert plans for the D.C.-area “Triumphal Arch” to “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” which could be used for snipers and drone storage.
articles.body: President Donald Trump said in a Truth Social post Sunday that he would convert plans for a Washington, D.C.-area “Triumphal Arch” to those for “a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch” at the request of the U.S. military, citing “national security.” The new plan, he said, is to “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage.” Reached for comment, a Pentagon spokesperson said the department has “nothing additional to provide beyond the post.” The White House declined to provide additional information. His post marked a significant change in plans that had already been in progress, as the Trump administration had announced earlier this month that it was preparing to break ground in the coming weeks. The president’s announcement was also the second time he has framed a controversial construction project as a national security endeavor. Trump previously argued that the White House ballroom construction was necessary for national security and tied the project to an underground military complex. The ballroom, too, has faced legal pushback, though the Supreme Court ruled at the end of August that the administration could move forward on ballroom construction indefinitely. The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued over the ballroom, arguing that Trump did not have the unilateral ability to undertake the project. The Supreme Court, though, ruled that the trust likely did not have proper standing to bring the case forward. In early April, the White House argued to a federal appeals court that the project, including the ballroom, was “necessary to ensure the safety and security of the White House and its grounds.” Weeks later, a gunman stormed a security checkpoint at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, prompting the president to issue renewed calls for a White House event space. The annual dinner is hosted by the White House Correspondents’ Association, not the White House. The proposed 250-foot arch project, which would sit in a roundabout between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, has faced legal challenges from veterans and historians. The project area sits on the Potomac, across from Washington. The arch proposal has already passed key hurdles, though it’s unclear how Trump’s announcement could affect the prior approvals. In April, the project obtained approval from the Commission of Fine Arts, which is now composed of the president’s allies after he fired previous members. In July, the National Capital Planning Commission, which is led by Trump appointees, approved the preliminary site and building plans. The arch, which would sit a few miles from Reagan airport, also passed the Federal Aviation Administration’s air safety standards last week, with the administration announcing that it “would not pose a hazard to aircraft.” Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., whose district includes Arlington National Cemetery and is adjacent to the proposed site, slammed Trump’s plan in a post to X. “Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea,” he said in the post. The project appeared poised to move forward imminently. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced on Sept. 3 that the administration was preparing to start excavation work “over the next two-week period.” U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan ordered the Trump administration to provide 48 hours’ notice before it starts “any activity” on the arch, other than work to determine whether there are archaeological resources on the proposed site. Trump has made Washington-area construction projects a key priority during his second term. Besides plans for the ballroom and arch, the president also moved to renovate the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, added a White House helipad and pushed to fix fountains in the capital. Following the renovation of the Reflecting Pool, chunks of the pool’s new coating floated to the surface and the water turned green with algae. Trump also repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that vandalism led to the damage.

articles.title: A commitment to the First Amendment should not be controversial
articles.summary: Across the country, I work with people and organizations that disagree profoundly about politics and public policy but share a basic principle: Americans must remain free to speak, associate, support causes and challenge those in power. That principle is being tested in uncomfortable ways. President Trump has threatened the Center for American Progress with a $5 billion…
articles.body:
Across the country, I work with people and organizations that disagree profoundly about politics and public policy but share a basic principle: Americans must remain free to speak, associate, support causes and challenge those in power.

That principle is being tested in uncomfortable ways.

President Trump has threatened the Center for American Progress with a $5 billion lawsuit over a report questioning whether National Guard deployments reduced violent crime. He has also publicly singled out some of the organizations and individuals that have supported the progressive think tank.

The center has responded that disagreements over public policy should be resolved through “robust public debate, not through threats or intimidation.” Whether you agree with its politics or its conclusions is beside the point. On this principle, it is right.

Government officials should not use their power to intimidate private organizations because they dislike their research or policy positions. And people should not have to wonder whether supporting an organization that challenges a president, governor or attorney general will make them a target as well. But the principle thatthe Center for American Progress invokes should extend beyond this dispute.

Unfortunately, even as it defends its own ability to challenge political power, the Center for American Progress is promoting a state-level initiative that would prohibit other groups from doing the same thing in elections and ballot referenda. Called the Corporate Power Reset , the proposal would withdraw from corporations, including nonprofit corporations, the right to spend their resources on certain election-related advocacy protected by the First Amendment.

That proposal would not have prohibited the center from publishing its National Guard report. But if preventing corporate political influence is a sufficient reason to silence nonprofit voices in elections, then it is only a matter of time before that same justification is turned against nonprofits that speak about public policy.

Moreover, elections and ballot measures are part of the robust public debate the Center for American Progress rightly says America needs.

Consider a governor campaigning for a ballot initiative that would dramatically expand state authority in some areas — perhaps even to activate the National Guard. He can travel the state, command media attention and urge voters to approve it. An incorporated nonprofit that believes the measure threatens civil liberties may want to spend its own resources urging voters to reject it. Under the center’s proposal, it would be legally prohibited from doing so.

Preventing nonprofits from speaking about ballot measures does nothing to help voters or make elections fairer. It just gives political leaders more wiggle room to force through their agenda without public discussion or pushback. The same is true in candidate elections. Politicians do not lose their platforms when private organizations are restricted. That imbalance should concern Americans on the political left and the right.

The government possesses powers private organizations never will. It can tax, regulate, investigate, prosecute and compel. When the government gains greater authority over private institutions’ ability to participate in political debate, the result is not a more neutral public square. It is a public square in which those who already hold political power can muscle out their opponents and critics.

Trump’s targeting of the Center for American Progress is a preview of what that looks like. It also illustrates why freedom of association matters. The center chooses to disclose many of its supporters publicly. It has every right to do so. But when a president responds to an organization’s criticism by publicly identifying some of its financial supporters, it becomes easy to understand why other organizations might choose differently.

Some Americans are comfortable publicly attaching their names to controversial causes. Others may worry about retaliation from government officials, employers, customers or activists. The possibility of retaliation can discourage people from supporting organizations long before anyone actually retaliates. That is why private giving should always remain a choice.

There is a fundamental inconsistency in defending an organization’s First Amendment rights when government power is directed against it while simultaneously advocating policies that would restrict the political participation of other organizations. But this moment should be about more than pointing out hypocrisy.

Trump’s threats against the Center for American Progress are bad for public discourse. So are efforts to give the government greater authority to decide when private organizations may use their resources to participate in elections. Both should remind us why constitutional principles cannot depend on who happens to hold power or whose speech we happen to like.

Today, a Republican president is threatening a progressive think tank. Tomorrow, a Democratic governor could target a conservative nonprofit. Political power changes hands. The rules protecting those who challenge it must endure.

The answer to powerful politicians is not to weaken the institutions capable of challenging them. We need a renewed commitment to protecting the freedom of Americans, individually and together, to speak, associate and answer those who wield government power.

Heather Lauer is CEO of People United for Privacy Foundation.

articles.body: President Donald Trump said Sunday that his planned triumphal arch near the Arlington Memorial Bridge will be converted into a military complex capable of housing drones, deploying snipers and storing ammunition. "At the strong request of the United States Military, and for National Security purposes, I have agreed to convert the magnificent Triumphal Arch … into a top grade Military Complex/Triumphal Arch," Trump wrote on Truth Social. TRUMP REVEALS ARC DE TRIOMPHE-STYLE MONUMENT FOR AMERICA’S 250TH ANNIVERSARY Trump said the 250-foot structure would have the "rapid ability" to deploy large numbers of drones, as well as snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition." "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World," Trump wrote. The monument, inspired by Paris’ Arc de Triomphe, is intended to welcome visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the nation’s capital. The proposed structure would be clad in granite and topped with three golden statues. FROM THE GILDED OVAL OFFICE TO A NEW BALLROOM: A LOOK AT TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE PROJECTS The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery. Opponents have also questioned whether the project requires congressional approval under federal law. The National Capital Planning Commission has approved the site and preliminary plans, but the project still requires additional review. Construction was previously expected to begin this month. The arch is one of several major construction and renovation projects Trump has pursued in Washington. TRUMP GAVE THE OVAL OFFICE A GILDED MAKEOVER – AND COVERED THE COST HIMSELF The administration has also begun work on a 90,000-square-foot White House ballroom. The sprawling addition, announced last July, will accommodate approximately 650 seated guests and follow the White House’s classical design. The White House currently lacks a formal ballroom, and the new structure is expected to replace the existing East Wing. Then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the ballroom is estimated to cost $200 million and will be financed by Trump and private donors. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The ballroom is not the only update. Trump has introduced gold accents in the Oval Office and Cabinet Room, lined the "walk of fame" with portraits of former presidents, including a photo of the autopen representing former President Joe Biden’s time in office, added stone pavers to the Rose Garden lawn and installed two 88-foot flagpoles. articles.title: Trump says planned 250-foot arch will be ‘military complex’ for drones, snipers
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Sunday said his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch will now be a “top grade” military complex that will house drones, snipers and amm...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Sunday said his proposed 250-foot triumphal arch will now be a "top grade" military complex that will house drones, snipers and ammunition.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump wrote that he has agreed to convert the arch "at the strong request" of the U.S. military, and "for National Security purposes."

The "Military Complex/Triumphal Arch" near Arlington National Cemetery will "house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage," Trump wrote. "There will be no facility like this anywhere in the World."

Trump's new claims about the arch, which come as veterans groups, historic preservationists and others attempt to stop the project, resemble his arguments for the need to build a ballroom at the White House. Trump initially said the ballroom was needed to entertain guests but more recently has said it was a "desperately needed National Security structure." That argument also has become central to the administration's legal claims that the ballroom must be built.

The Trump administration, which plans to begin construction on the arch as soon as November, has been consulting with D.C.'s and Virginia's historic preservation offices as part of a required federal preservation process. The National Capital Planning Commission previously said the arch is intended to be a "visitor destination" with an observation deck.

The topic of converting the arch to a military complex has not previously been raised, even as the project has undergone months of federally required reviews.

The White House did not immediately respond to questions about the president's post. The Interior Department, which oversees the federal parkland where the arch would be built, did not immediately reply to requests for comment, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond the president's post.

Trump has spent nearly a year touting his plans to build an arch at Memorial Circle, a traffic roundabout tucked inside Washington's boundaries, near the entrance to the military cemetery and managed by the National Park Service.

The president and his deputies have said the arch should be built to commemorate the nation's 250th anniversary. The administration contends it does not need congressional approval for the arch because lawmakers a century ago authorized a somewhat similar project near the site.

"This will be one of the Great Pieces of American Architecture, honoring the history and significance of Arlington Cemetery and befitting the most powerful Capital in the World," Interior Secretary Doug Burgum wrote on X this month.

Trump's plan for the arch has been opposed by military veterans, historic preservationists and local activists, who have said the towering structure would overshadow the cemetery, alter pedestrians' views of the Lincoln Memorial and other historic sites, and cause other disruptions.

A D.C. official last week advised the administration to abandon its planned arch and instead pursue a less obtrusive alternative.

Some preservationists and advocates questioned Sunday whether the project would now need to undergo additional reviews, if its purpose is being significantly changed. They also questioned the practicality of constructing a military complex at the center of a widely used traffic circle not far from Reagan National Airport.

"Putting a drone launching site directly in the landing path for DCA is a stupid, dangerous, and unworkable idea," Rep. Don Beyer (D-Virginia), who represents the district that encompasses the airport, said on X, suggesting the plan was a legal pretext.

"The President's belated efforts to manufacture a national security justification for this project do nothing to cure its fundamental illegality," said Nicolas Sansone, a lawyer at Public Citizen Litigation Group, a watchdog organization that is representing several veterans who say the large arch would alter their experience when visiting the nearby military cemetery.

A federal judge has been weighing whether to halt the project. U.S. District Judge Tanya S. Chutkan, an Obama appointee, has also warned the Trump administration not to abruptly move forward with construction on the arch - as Trump did when demolishing the White House's East Wing to build his ballroom without seeking approval from federal review panels or from Congress.

Trump officials have said they will obtain "all necessary approvals" before beginning construction on the arch.

The president's claim Sunday about the arch being converted to a military complex follows his administration's evolving legal strategy to defend the ballroom on similar grounds.

Administration officials have increasingly contended that the ballroom must be built by citing the planned military complex being constructed underneath it and the need to protect the president.

Judge Neomi Rao, a Trump appointee to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, said the administration's national security claims in the ballroom case had merit.

"The equities in this case turn on complex architectural and security determinations best made by the Secret Service and the military - not judges," Rao wrote in August.

Other federal judges have said that Trump could not claim broad national security reasons as a basis to pursue a construction project that had not been authorized by Congress.

"While I take seriously the Government's concerns regarding the safety and security of the White House grounds and the President himself, the existence of a 'large hole' beside the White House is, of course, a problem of the President's own making," U.S. District Judge Richard Leon - who first blocked work on the ballroom - wrote earlier this year.

The Supreme Court on Aug. 31 ruled 5-4 that construction on the ballroom could continue for now but declined to rule on the merits of the administration's arguments in that case.

articles.title: Trump on Iran: ‘My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up?’
articles.summary: President Trump on Sunday speculated on the future of the Iran war, asking “if and when do I blow the entire nation up?” Fox News’s Trey Yingst reported that Trump is in a “deciding mode” and “that very big things are going to be happening in the not so distant future.” “The president described the…
articles.body:
President Trump on Sunday speculated on the future of the Iran war , asking “if and when do I blow the entire nation up?”

Fox News’s Trey Yingst reported that Trump is in a “deciding mode” and “that very big things are going to be happening in the not so distant future.”

“The president described the current choices on the table as ‘wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically or making a deal,” Yingst said. “He added, ‘My question is if and when do I blow the entire nation up? They better behave.'”

Trump said Thursday that he’s weighing the decision to “go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not,” he told Axios, adding that anything “could happen with me.”

The comments come after reports surfaced that Trump is expected to meet with six Persian Gulf leaders on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly this week. The Trump administration will also allow a “core delegation” of Iranian officials, like Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, to attend the high-level session at the General Assembly.

It is the latest iteration of Trump’s threat to devastate Iran. He warned in April that “a whole civilization will die” unless “maybe something revolutionarily wonderful can happen.” This threat, attached to a deadline, prompted talks with Iran and a brief ceasefire.

The U.S.-Israeli conflict in Iran has caused energy prices to skyrocket worldwide, pushing the national average for gas prices to $4.48 as of Sunday, according to AAA . Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital shipping lane for oil exports, has primarily led to prices rising for almost seven months.

But Trump has frequently downplayed the high gas prices after long praising their lows prior to the initial U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran on Feb. 28.

“It’s a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done. Remember that. It’s a little more. Frankly, even if it was a lot more,” Trump said at a rally for Republican Senate nominee Michael Whatley in Gastonia on Wednesday. “But that’s going to come tumbling down. That’s going to be like rocket ships in reverse.”

Republican lawmakers have been put on the defensive on the issue as they face Democrats making the cost of living a core issue going into the midterm elections.

“As I’m talking to Alaskans, they’re saying, ‘Wait a minute, he said we were going to be in and out in a matter of weeks,'” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) said last week. “And not only are we still there but this is what I am feeling in my community when it comes to the cost of the war. I’m not satisfied with where we are. Not at all.”

articles.title: Moore says Trump uses Constitution like a ‘suggestion box’ in banning CNN, Politico, MS NOW reporters from White House
articles.summary: Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Sunday accused President Trump of using the Constitution as a “suggestion box” with his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters covering the White House. Moore said in an interview on “State of the Union” with CNN’s Dana Bash that Trump “seems to have a real problem” with…
articles.body:
Maryland Gov. Wes Moore (D) on Sunday accused President Trump of using the Constitution as a “suggestion box” with his ban on CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters covering the White House.

Moore said in an interview on “State of the Union” with CNN’s Dana Bash that Trump “seems to have a real problem” with free speech, voting rights and states’ rights as defined in the Constitution.

“And, again, not even just clearly laid out, that, at the founding of this nation, that the founding fathers of this country found it to be so important that they made things like the freedom of the press and free speech and freedom of assembly so important that they made it the First Amendment, the first thing they wanted to get done in this country,” Moore continued.

The Maryland Democrat added that Trump “continues to use the Constitution like it is a suggestion box simply because he does not like the coverage.”

“And so I would just hope that this administration would spend a little bit of time reading, instead of just talking,” he said.

U.S. Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz defended the president’s decision to ban reporters earlier in the broadcast. He told Bash that the president is “ absolutely within his rights ” to ban the three outlets’ White House reporters from covering him in person.

“I would hope that the media would take a good introspective look at itself and its practices, because it throws things out there and then puts a little baby correction that nobody pays attention to, and it sticks to people like napalm,” Waltz said, later prompting pushback from Bash.

Trump announced the ban via Truth Social on Friday, posting that it went into immediate effect “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!” He later warned that other outlets could be banned in the future.

CNN, Politico and MS NOW reporters were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday. All three outlets denounced the ban , and MS NOW said it will “take any and all steps necessary” to protect its reporters’ First Amendment right to report on the president.

Weijia Jiang, former president of the White House Correspondents’ Association and CBS News senior White House correspondent, told Bash that the media’s response to the ban was “not a tantrum by three media outlets because the journalists are upset.”

“This is a restriction of information that we work so tirelessly to gather, to give to the public,” she said. “And an attack on one media organization is an attack on all media organizations because it could be us next. The individual outlets matter less than what the president is trying to do. He is very explicit about it.”

articles.title: Puigdemont pide un referéndum para Ceuta y Melilla: “Dos colonias o ciudades dentro de Marruecos"
articles.standfirst: El ex presidente de la Generalitat concedió una entrevista al diario británico The Sunday Times
articles.summary: El ex presidente de la Generalitat concedió una entrevista al diario británico The Sunday Times
articles.body: Polémica respecto a las últimas declaraciones del ex presidente de la Generalitat de Cataluña Carles Puigdemont, ahora mismo residiendo en Waterloo, Bélgica. El de Junts per Catalunya habló sobre Ceuta y Melilla en una entrevista para el medio de Reino Unido The Sunday Times. En ella, pide un referéndum de autodeterminación para ambas ciudades autónomas, además de calificarlas como "dos colonias o ciudades dentro de Marruecos". Según explica, entiende que el Gobierno marroquí entienda esos dos enclaves como “una herida". “¿Qué sentido tiene para un país de la Unión Europea tener dos colonias o dos ciudades en Marruecos? Si lo miras desde una perspectiva marroquí, por supuesto que esto es una herida”, fueron sus palabras exactas. Eso sí, deja claro que los ceutíes son "muy españoles", aunque no ve con malos ojos un referéndum sobre su futuro: “Se vería legitimada si celebrasen un referéndum de autodeterminación", idea trasladada desde la situación en Cataluña. Momento que usa para llevarlo al tema catalán: "Temen que nosotros pidamos también un referéndum", explicó, asegurando que el ejecutivo español podría sentar un precedente para otras zonas de España si esto se llevase a cabo. Posteriormente, habló de su situación personal desde su salida de territorio nacional en 2017: "Yo no sabía cuánto tiempo iba a pasar en el exilio, pero estaba dispuesto a pasar mi vida entera. Y si tengo que pasar mi vida entera, estoy dispuesto", de hecho, desde que está fuera, no ha podido vivir el fallecimiento de sus padres. También se refiere a un posible retorno a España, señalando: “Lo primero que me he propuesto, si puedo volver, una cosa que aún está por ver, es sumergirme en la Catalunya de hoy. Esta es mi primera intención: respirarla, tocarla, escucharla... y verlo todo con mis propios ojos”, explicó. Es más, en varias ocasiones antes ya había hablado de una gira por Cataluña en caso de poder volver.

articles.title: Why Trump zeroed in on Greenland, the world’s largest island, mostly covered in ice — in 3 charts
articles.summary: President Donald Trump says his Greenland deal gives the U.S. permanent control over the island's security while barring China and Russia from Arctic footholds.
articles.body: President Donald Trump’s Greenland push has moved from threats to a new security agreement with Denmark and Greenland that he says will give the United States "permanent control" over the island’s security and allow Washington to expand its military presence there. The agreement still requires approval from Danish and Greenlandic lawmakers. Its full terms have not been made public, but officials say it would leave Greenland under Danish sovereignty while barring China, Russia and other non-NATO adversaries from establishing military bases or making certain sensitive investments on the island. TRUMP THREATENS TARIFFS ON COUNTRIES OPPOSING GREENLAND TAKEOVER PLANS Greenland rarely draws global attention. But as Arctic ice melts and great powers compete for influence, the world’s largest island has become a strategic prize. A semi-autonomous territory of Denmark, Greenland is home to a key U.S. military base and sits near emerging shipping routes and critical mineral deposits. Greenland’s roughly 56,000 residents are spread across five municipalities, with most living in small coastal towns. About 80% of the island is covered by an ice sheet, leaving much of its vast interior uninhabited. Despite its small population, Greenland is nearly the size of Alaska and Texas combined. Its location off Canada’s northeastern coast places Greenland at the heart of Arctic defense planning. The U.S. has maintained a military outpost in northwestern Greenland since 1953 at Pituffik Space Base, now operated by the U.S. Space Force. Russia also maintains military installations in the region, while China has sought greater access since declaring itself a "near-Arctic state" in 2018. Retreating Arctic ice is opening shipping lanes around the island that could shorten trade routes between North America, Europe and Asia. The changing landscape has also drawn attention to Greenland’s rare earth elements and other critical minerals used in technology, renewable energy and military systems. CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS Rare earth elements are especially important in high-performance magnets used in electric vehicles, wind turbines, generators and precision-guidance systems. They are also used in missile guidance, radar, sonar, satellites and advanced aircraft. China dominates the global rare-earth supply chain, accounting for roughly 60% of mining and more than 90% of processing capacity. As the U.S. and European Union seek to reduce their reliance on Beijing, Greenland has emerged as a potential counterweight. As competition over shipping routes, defense positioning and critical minerals intensifies, Greenland’s importance is likely to grow.

articles.title: Florida Republican says Trump ‘has his own style’ in handling reporters covering the White House
articles.summary: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) on Sunday said President Trump “has his own style” in handling reporters who cover him, defending his move to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW‘s reporters from the White House. “I think that he has his own style and that he will determine who he wants to talk to, but…
articles.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) on Sunday said President Trump “has his own style” in handling reporters who cover him, defending his move to ban CNN, Politico and MS NOW ‘s reporters from the White House.

“I think that he has his own style and that he will determine who he wants to talk to, but with social media and with all the different outlets out there for people to receive information, I am sure that those journalists are going to be able to cover the president the way that you –– you know, free speech, the way you determine,” Salazar told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation.”

Salazar, who worked for the Spanish-language outlet Telemundo for 30 years and worked at CNN Español and Univision, echoed other Republicans and administration officials by calling Trump “the most accessible president in [recent] years that has been talking to the media.”

“So he may not be allowing for some journalists to go into one place, but I’m sure that he’s got to be talking to everybody at some point,” she said. “That’s his style and he’s very accessible, not like [former President] Biden.”

The Florida Republican later suggested to Brennan that the “American school of journalism is not so vigorous as it was during the time that we started this career. So I have my different opinions as to what’s happening on television.”

Trump announced the ban via Truth Social on Friday, posting that it went into immediate effect “as a result of their constant ‘reportin’ FAKE NEWS!” He later warned that other outlets could be banned in the future.

All three outlets denounced the ban , as reporters from CNN, Politico and MS NOW were denied access to the White House grounds on Saturday.

Weijia Jiang, CBS News’s senior White House correspondent and former president of the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA), told her WHCA successor and “Fox News Sunday” host Jacqui Heinrich that the outlets’ response was “not a tantrum” over the ban but “a serious concern for the public.”

“Look, every administration, every president hates the press,” Jiang said. “There should be tension. We wouldn’t be doing our jobs and, neither would they, if there wasn’t that friction.”

Jiang warned that Trump drawing this “red line” opens the door for future administrations “who might do the same on the other side of it,” a possibility she called “worrisome.”

CNN telegraphed potential legal action if Trump made good on his promise to keep its reporters from the White House, while MS NOW stated that it will “take any and all steps necessary” to protect its reporters’ constitutional right to report on the president.

Politico pushed back on Trump’s claim, in the Truth Social post where he declared the ban, that Politico receives $8 million in government subsidies for its “Politico Pro subscription.” The outlet denied this, saying that these claims were “false and have been thoroughly debunked.”

articles.title: Nicki Minaj offers career advice to young Americans, delivers blunt response to Trump critics

articles.body: Rapper Nicki Minaj shared her career advice to young Americans entering the workforce and fiercely defended her support of President Donald Trump during an exclusive interview with "The Ingraham Angle" on Friday. The music mogul opened up about her journey to the top, explaining how she hustled her way from serving biscuits at Red Lobster to dominating music charts around the world and collaborating with some of the biggest names in Hollywood. "I did customer service for telephone companies. I was a telemarketer. I sold fire extinguishers. I did everything," Minaj shared with Fox News. NICKI MINAJ, ANNA NICOLE SMITH AND MORE STARS WHO GOT THEIR START WAITING TABLES AT RED LOBSTER MARY J BLIGE CREDITS FAITH, PASTORS WITH CONFRONTING HER PRIDE AS SHE TOOK CONTROL OF HER CAREER "What I would tell young people is: This is not the best part of your life, but it is probably one of the most important parts of your life," she said. "All the people skills, and the communication skills, and all the problem-solving that I learned then, it still applies now when I'm around superstars or rich people." "All of those skills, they carry over into the rest of your life. So don't look at that part of your life as something that you can't wait to fly by because… you might not be making the biggest money, but you're doing the real nitty-gritty work that is going to help you for the rest of your life," Minaj added. THE RICH HAVE ONE FINANCIAL HABIT MOST AMERICANS IGNORE AT THEIR PERIL The "Super Bass" and "Starships" singer, who has an estimated net worth of $150 million according to Celebrity Net Worth, also advised young Americans to save money, saying that "no matter how little" she made, she would always set aside funds for a rainy day. Minaj also discussed her support for President Donald Trump after emerging as one of his fiercest allies in Hollywood. The rapper recently partnered with the Trump administration on the Small Business Administration’s Million Dollar Pitch Competition, serving as one of the celebrity judges. LIL WAYNE PRAISES TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM PROJECT, CALLS OUT CRITICS WHO 'DON'T KNOW NOTHING' The competition brought five small business owners before a panel of judges, including Minaj and Airbnb’s co-founder, to give their best pitch for a share of a $1 million cash prize pool. "Small business represents the heart of the country…," said Minaj. "You don't have to be a huge household name to be recognized by the president and to be recognized by us." DOLLY PARTON REFUSED TO PICK POLITICAL SIDES FOR DECADES: ‘I’M NOT IN POLITICS, I’M AN ENTERTAINER’ "He's very grounded. It's easy to connect with him, it's easy feel like he heard you, he understands you," she continued. "And I just love him, and I'm not going to ever make excuses for that." Minaj was also asked when her fans, whom she fondly refers to as "Barbz," can expect her next tour following a hiatus after her Pink Friday 2 World Tour in 2024. articles.title: Trump set to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday
articles.summary: President Donald Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani for a third time on Monday
articles.body: President Donald Trump will meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Monday, the mayor’s office confirmed to NBC News. In a statement, Mamdani’s office said the two would meet at Gracie Mansion, the mayor’s official residence, to discuss “issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers.” The president will be in New York City for the United Nations General Assembly meeting, where he is set to deliver remarks on Tuesday and meet with global leaders. This will be at least the third public meeting between Trump and Mamdani, who have previously met at the White House. The two first met in November 2025. The Democratic mayor, who was first elected almost a year ago, and the president have had a mostly friendly relationship, though they have at times publicly criticized each other. Prior to their first meeting, Trump described Mamdani as a “communist lunatic,” but after meeting with the then-mayor-elect in the Oval Office, the president told reporters that he’d be “cheering” for Mamdani and described him as a “very rational person.” In an April interview with NBC News’ “Meet the Press,” Mamdani called his relationship with Trump “honest, direct and productive.” He added that the pair get along as two natives of the nation’s largest city, saying, “New York City holds a very special place for him as well as for me. We’re both from the same city.” Following their second White House meeting in February, Mamdani said he raised to the president the arrest of a Columbia University student by Department of Homeland Security agents. The student was released shortly after their meeting. Despite Trump maintaining a chummier relationship with Mamdani than with other Democrats, the president has jabbed at him publicly. Earlier this year, Mamdani rolled out his plan to impose a pied-à-terre tax on New York City homeowners who maintain a nonprimary residence in the city. Trump derided the tax as “SO WRONG” in a post on Truth Social, writing, “Sadly, Mayor Mamdani is DESTROYING New York! It has no chance! The United States of America should not contribute to its failure. It will only get WORSE. The TAX, TAX, TAX Policies are SO WRONG.” During his campaign last year, Mamdani called the president a “despot” and a “fascist,” remarks he defended even after his first meeting with Trump. “That’s something I’ve said in the past and I say today,” he told “Meet the Press” after the Oval Office meeting. “I think what I appreciated about the conversation that I had with the president was that we were not shy about the places of disagreement, about the politics that has brought us to this moment,” the mayor added. “And we also wanted to focus on what it could look like to deliver on a shared analysis of an affordability crisis for New Yorkers.” Mamdani has also criticized Trump’s decision to go to war with Iran. In April, he blamed the military conflict for worsening a cost-of-living crisis in the city he leads. “I wish that the words of Tupac from the ’90s weren’t still prescient, but they continue to be true for too many, which is that ‘We always have money for war and not to feed the poor,’” he told “Meet the Press.”

President Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) are set to meet Monday at the mayor’s house, Gracie Mansion, in the Big Apple, a White House official and the mayor’s press office said Sunday.

In an emailed statement, Mamdani’s press office said that “the meeting will focus on issues affecting New York City and New Yorkers.”

Mamdani and Trump, while on opposite sides of the political spectrum, have had a notably cordial relationship.

Earlier this year , Mamdani touted a “productive” meeting with the president at the White House, in which the mayor said they talked about the possibility of building additional housing in the two politicians’ hometown.

Trump also praised the then-mayor-elect following another meeting last November at the White House. The president had previously attacked the democratic socialist, who ran an insurgent campaign against former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, and called Mamdani a “communist.”

“I think you’re going to have, hopefully, a really great mayor. The better he does, the happier I am,” Trump said at the time in the Oval Office, with Mamdani right next to him.

“There’s no difference in party, there’s no difference in anything. And we’re going to be helping him to make everybody’s dream come true. Having a strong and very safe New York.”

In the wake of Mamdani’s win last year, democratic socialists and left-leaning candidates have notched wins in Democratic primaries across the country. The New York City mayor has also rapidly become one of the most prominent Democrats in the country and a target for the right.

articles.title: Hassett on Iran war: ‘The president had to act’
articles.summary: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Sunday defended President Trump’s handling of the Iran war and said the president “had to act,” suggesting that otherwise the outcome could have been dire. “The whole thing started because the Iranians told us we don’t have to talk to you anymore, because we’re two weeks from having…
articles.body:
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Sunday defended President Trump’s handling of the Iran war and said the president “had to act,” suggesting that otherwise the outcome could have been dire.

“The whole thing started because the Iranians told us we don’t have to talk to you anymore, because we’re two weeks from having a nuclear weapon,” Hassett told Fox News’s Peter Doocy on “The Sunday Briefing.” “And you see that [they’re] shooting ships like crazy in the straits and everything; the president had to act.”

Hassett added that if “you think about what would have happened if he hadn’t acted, then it would be really, really bad for the global economy, for human civilization.”

The director said the U.S. Navy is bringing up to 1 billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial route for exported goods like crude oil. He suggested that this was keeping prices “as low as it could possibly be, given the disruption.”

“People, when this started, were saying, ‘We’re going to have $150, $200 oil, and we haven’t had that because President Trump organized everybody to get friendly oil out of the straits,” Hassett continued. “And meanwhile, Iran isn’t getting any oil out of the straits, and they’re running out of money, they’re having hyper inflation and their economy’s totally on the ropes.”

U.S. forces have supported the transport of over 1 billion barrels of crude oil through the strait “in the last couple of months,” according to U.S. Central Command (Centcom) commander Adm. Brad Cooper on Saturday.

The strait, which carries around a fifth of the world’s oil consumption daily under normal conditions, was effectively shut off by Iran since the U.S. and Israel launched the conflict with Iran in late February.

Gas prices have risen since, with the national average in the U.S. reaching $4.48 as of Saturday, up 17 cents since last week, according to AAA . The average for diesel reached $6.50, also as of Saturday.

President Trump and his administration have downplayed the conflict’s effect on gas prices. The president said on Wednesday at a campaign rally in North Carolina that the rising cost of gas was “a very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done. Remember that.” Trump has also sought to cast blame on energy facilities hit as part of the Russia-Ukraine war.

But the high cost of gas and diesel is proving to be the latest economic headache for Republicans heading into the midterm elections. They have struggled to address gas prices, but diesel could be more difficult, as the rising costs hit key members of the GOP base like rural voters.

The party has encouraged incumbents and candidates to talk about the passage of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, also known as the Working Families Tax Cuts, as well as efforts to lower prescription drug prices.

articles.title: Florida Republican calls interim Venezuelan president ‘necessary evil’
articles.summary: Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) on Sunday called Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez a “necessary evil” until the Latin American country can have free and fair elections. Salazar defended President Trump’s decision to meet with Rodríguez in New York City, while Trump is present for the annual United Nations General Assembly. She told CBS News’s…
articles.body:
Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar (R-Fla.) on Sunday called Venezuela’s interim president Delcy Rodríguez a “necessary evil” until the Latin American country can have free and fair elections.

Salazar defended President Trump’s decision to meet with Rodríguez in New York City, while Trump is present for the annual United Nations General Assembly. She told CBS News’s Margaret Brennan on “Face the Nation” that the president has created a “new blueprint” on “how to deal with dictators.”

“Just like [Secretary of State Marco] Rubio said recently, that there was recovery trends and then transition,” Salazar said. “I do know that the United States is in the business to bringing liberty and democracy to our neighbors and transition will occur. So Delcy is just a necessary evil, for now, to stabilize.”

She added that Trump “liberated” Venezuela’s people “from socialism, from disaster, from misery.”

“Now, I’m sure that, soon, we’re going to be able to create new and fair elections,” the Florida Republican continued. “These international observers –– and once again, we will have done our job, to bring democracy and freedom to the Western Hemisphere.”

Rodríguez, previously Venezuela’s vice president, was elevated to her interim role after a surprise U.S. military raid captured President Nicolás Maduro in January to face drug trafficking charges in the U.S.

She has condemned Trump and the U.S. for Maduro’s capture, but she has also praised the relationship that developed over exporting oil out of her oil-rich country, set down in a recent major deal.

Trump has praised Rodríguez as someone who wants to “make Venezuela great again.” In April, the administration lifted sanctions on her, removing Rodríguez from the Office of Foreign Assets Control’s Specially Designated Nationals List. She was added to the list in 2018 for allegedly weakening Venezuela’s democracy.

Salazar has called out Rodríguez before, but recently she spoke out against the reported federal detention of exiled Venezuelan journalist Luis Galeano in Miami. The Venezuelan government stripped Galeano’s citizenship due to his criticism of the regime, and his U.S. asylum application has been pending for seven years.

She urged the administration that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “enforce the law and deport dangerous individuals, but do not treat political exiles like criminals.”

Salazar is running against Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez in the state’s 27th Congressional District, which she was first elected to in 2020. The district includes parts of Miami and is home to one of the highest foreign-born populations of any House district.

articles.title: DDHQ director says Mike Rogers’s time is ‘running out’
articles.summary: Scott Tranter, Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) director of data science, on Sunday said that “time is running out” for Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers to close the gap between him and Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed. DDHQ’s forecast shows El-Sayed with a 67 percent probability of winning in November, with Rogers holding a 33 percent…
articles.body:
Scott Tranter, Decision Desk HQ’s (DDHQ) director of data science, on Sunday said that “time is running out” for Republican Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers to close the gap between him and Democratic opponent Abdul El-Sayed.

DDHQ’s forecast shows El-Sayed with a 67 percent probability of winning in November, with Rogers holding a 33 percent chance. Tranter told NewsNation’s Chris Stirewalt on “The Hill Sunday” that “this one is closer than it should be if you’re the Republicans and want to keep the Senate.”

“El-Sayed’s got the momentum. It’s pretty undeniable,” he said. “Michigan’s going to start voting in about a month on the early side. And look, everything you know about Michigan –– about a third of that voing to come in before Election Day. So Mike Rogers’s time is running out.”

Stirewalt and Tranter agreed that El-Sayed’s support from former Vice President Kamala Harris will be a problem for him, referring to the opposition she faced from pro-Palestinian voters in an uproar over the Biden administration’s support for Israel during the 2024 presidential election. El-Sayed has spoken out against the Israeli government and shown support for the Palestinians in Gaza.

Harris is expected to join El-Sayed, a physician, at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health on Tuesday. El-Sayed told Politico last Wednesday that Black maternal health is an issue they have both been “a leader on,” and he called the former vice president an “inspirational leader.”

More than a dozen Michigan rabbis and Jewish leaders launched a petition earlier this month to push El-Sayed to alter his rhetoric on Israel. They called for him to affirm Jewish safety, that Israel has a right to exist and to encourage the Jewish community’s civic and political participation. The petition did not name El-Sayed, though it was clearly directed toward him.

Rogers did not attend a televised debate with El-Sayed last week and said he “ never agreed ” to it, which resulted in the Democrat speaking for one hour next to an empty podium. Rogers accused the moderator of showing bias toward El-Sayed — a claim the moderator, Fox 2 Detroit’s Roop Raj, has rejected and requested that Rogers appear for the sake of voters.

When asked by CBS News Detroit about critics suggesting the GOP candidate was unwilling to engage in a discussion with El-Sayed, Rogers said that two televised debates are scheduled for October.

Polling has shown the populist candidate holds a narrow lead over the Republican. The Hill/Emerson College Polling survey on Thursday showed El-Sayed at 48 percent compared to Rogers’s 46 percent. Four percent of respondents said they were still undecided.
